summary: This unit teaches you to plan and apply make-up that suits the client, her skin and the occasion: consult and check for contraindications, prepare the skin, match foundation to skin tone and undertone, use colour theory and corrective make-up to balance the face, and apply day, evening and bridal looks hygienically. You will also learn to give aftercare advice, recommend products honestly and keep records.

blocks.p: Good make-up looks as if it belongs to the client. It suits her skin, her features, her outfit, the light she will be seen in and the occasion, and it lasts through Jamaica's heat. To achieve that you need more than a steady hand: you need to read skin, understand colour, know your products and plan the look before you start.
Make-up is also a close, personal service near the eyes and mouth, where infections pass easily. That is why this unit is about **hygiene, safety and judgement** as much as artistry.

What this means in the salon

Good light close to daylight; a disinfected trolley laid out in order
Hygienic handling of every product; clean and disinfected tools
Consult the client and check for contraindications
Find out the occasion, setting, outfit and look wanted
Ask about allergies, eye problems, contact lenses and health
Refer or adapt when needed; get the record card signed

Skin type, skin tone and undertone
Face shape and features that may need balancing
Design the look
Use colour theory to choose colours
Plan corrective make-up on a face chart

Apply the make-up
Correct, conceal and match the base; set it
Eyes, brows, lashes, cheeks and lips, blended and balanced

Day, evening, bridal, photographs and television

Aftercare and removal advice; honest product advice

flow: Set up the workstation
Consult and check for contraindications
Analyse skin and face
Plan the look on a face chart
Prepare the skin
Apply the make-up
Check, advise and record
Clean up

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and practical tasks in the Centre's salon. In the practical tasks you plan and apply a day make-up for a daytime event, and a corrective evening make-up for a special occasion, each planned on a face chart with a signed record card. The assessor watches your hygiene, consultation, colour choices, blending and clean-up as well as the finished look.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Photograph close-ups of the work (one eye, one cheek, the lips). Take a whole-face photo only if the client agrees in writing and the Centre allows it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Eye and lip infections, cold sores and skin infections pass easily on make-up, brushes and fingers. Every product that has touched a client, and every tool, must be handled so that nothing passes to the next client.

head: Word
What it means
In make-up
rows: Cleaning
Removing make-up, oil and dirt with soap, brush shampoo or detergent and water. It comes first.
Washing brushes and the palette; wiping the trolley.
Disinfecting
Using a chemical that kills most germs on clean tools and hard surfaces, left on for the contact time on its label.
Tweezers, lash curlers, sharpeners, spatulas (if reusable), the trolley.
Sterilising
Killing all germs, including spores, for example in an autoclave.
Metal tools such as tweezers, where the salon has the equipment.
Pathogen
A germ that can cause disease.
Bacteria in conjunctivitis and impetigo; the virus in cold sores.

head: Product
How to use it
rows: Creams, cream foundation, concealer in pots
Take out with a clean (or disposable) spatula onto a clean palette. Never put fingers or a used brush into the pot.
Lipstick
Scrape a little onto the palette with a disposable spatula; apply with a clean lip brush. Never apply straight from the tube.
Liquids
Pump or squeeze onto the palette or the back of your clean hand.
Pressed powders and eyeshadows
Use a clean brush, or scrape a little onto the palette for clients you are unsure of.
Mascara and lip gloss
A new disposable wand for every dip. Never put a used wand back into the tube.
Pencils
Sharpen before each client to give a fresh surface; wipe and disinfect the sharpener.
Sponges, cotton buds, wands, cotton pads
Single-use: throw away after the client.

blocks.note: **Never double-dip.** Once a brush, wand or applicator has touched the client, it does not go back into a product.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Best practice is a clean set of brushes for each client.

If you must use one set for several clients, clean each brush between clients with a quick-drying brush cleaner as its maker says, wipe it on a clean tissue until no colour comes off, and let it dry before use.

At the end of the day deep-clean every brush: wash the bristles in brush shampoo or mild soap and lukewarm water, rinse with the bristles pointing down so water does not loosen the glue in the handle, squeeze out the water, reshape, and dry flat or bristles down. Disinfect as the brush and product makers allow.
Store clean brushes covered, away from dust and spray.
**Light:** bright, even light on the face, as close to daylight as possible, from the front. Light from above casts shadows; coloured or yellow light makes you misjudge colours.
**Chair:** a make-up chair at a height where you can work with a straight back; the client's head supported and comfortable.

**Trolley:** wiped with disinfectant and covered with clean paper or a towel; brushes, sponges, spatulas, palette, disposable wands, cotton pads, tissues, headband and gown laid out in the order you will use them.
**Waste:** a lined bin with a lid close by; a sharps box for sharpener blades.
**Paperwork:** the record card and a face chart ready.

blocks.note: Setting sprays, hairspray and brush cleaners are often alcohol-based or in aerosols: flammable. Keep them closed, away from heat, lamps and flames, and spray setting spray in a ventilated area with the client's eyes closed. Keep cables of lighted mirrors and ring lights tidy and away from drinks and water.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Heat and sun spoil make-up fast. Do not store your kit on a sunny shelf or leave it in a hot car: foundations separate, lipsticks melt, and germs grow faster in warm, used products.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: The **open-jar symbol** with a number such as '12M' means use the product within 12 months of opening it. Write the date you opened it on the pack. As a guide, mascara and liquid eyeliner are usually replaced about every 3 months, because they touch the eye; liquid foundations and lipsticks often last about a year; powders longer. Throw away anything that smells odd, has separated or has changed colour.
The consultation is a private conversation before you touch the client's face. Sit her in good light with her face clean or nearly clean, so you can see her skin as it is.

flow: Greet her and explain the consultation
Ask your questions
Look at the skin, face and eyes
Check for contraindications
Agree the look, products and price
Sketch the plan on a face chart
Record and get her signature

head: Ask about
Why it matters
rows: The occasion, time of day, indoors or outdoors, how long it must last
Decides the strength of the look and the products that will last.
Her outfit, accessories and hair
Colours should go with what she is wearing.
The look she likes and dislikes; photos she has saved
So that you design what she wants, not what you want.
Allergies, sensitive skin, past reactions to make-up or lash glue
To avoid ingredients that could cause a reaction.
Eye problems; contact lenses
Eye infections stop the service; lens wearers need gentle eye make-up.
Skin conditions, medicines, recent treatments (peels, laser, waxing, brow tint)
Some leave the skin sensitive or broken, so areas must be avoided.
Her usual routine and products
Helps you advise and choose products she will be able to keep up.

blocks.p: A **contraindication** is a condition that means a service should not go ahead, or must be changed. Infections stop the service; other conditions mean you avoid an area or adapt your products.

head: Condition
What you see
What you do
rows: Conjunctivitis
Red, sore, watery or sticky eye; crusts on the lashes.
No eye make-up; refer to a doctor or pharmacist. It spreads very easily.
Stye
A small, painful, pus-filled lump on the edge of an eyelid.
No eye make-up; refer.
Blepharitis
Red, swollen, crusty eyelid edges.
No eye make-up; refer.
Cold sore (herpes simplex)
Tingling, then blisters and crusts, usually on or near the lips.
Do not carry out the service; it spreads. Suggest she sees a doctor or pharmacist.
Impetigo, boils, ringworm or any skin infection
Weeping sores or honey-coloured crusts; red painful lumps; round scaly patches.
Do not carry out the service; refer.
Infected spots or razor bumps
Red bumps with yellow heads.
Avoid them completely; refer if widespread.
Cuts, grazes, bruising, swelling, recent scars
Broken or tender skin.
Avoid the area.
Sunburn, or skin red after a peel, laser or waxing
Red, hot, sore or peeling skin.
Avoid the area or postpone.
Eczema, psoriasis or dermatitis
Red, dry, flaky or itchy patches.
If unbroken and calm, work gently with mild, fragrance-free products; if broken or weeping, avoid; refer if severe.
Rash from a new product or known allergy
Raised, red, itchy skin.
Do not apply over it; avoid the product; suggest a doctor or pharmacist if it does not settle.

blocks.note: Do not name the condition or diagnose. Explain kindly and privately what you have seen, why the service cannot go ahead safely today, and who she should see. Record it.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Ask whether she would like to remove them before eye make-up; many clients prefer to keep them in.
Do not line the inner rim (waterline) of the eye, and avoid loose glitter and fibre mascaras that can fall into the eye.
Use products made for sensitive eyes, and tap off extra powder before it reaches the eye area.

blocks.p: For clients with sensitive skin or allergies, and before strip lash adhesive is used for the first time, a skin (patch) test is often done 24 to 48 hours before the service, behind the ear or in the crease of the elbow, following the product maker and the Centre's policy. Some lash adhesives contain latex. Record the result.
A **contra-action** is an unwanted reaction during or after the service: redness, itching, swelling, a burning or stinging feeling, a rash, or watering, sore eyes.

flow: Stop at once
Remove the product gently with cool water or a mild cleanser
Rinse an eye with plenty of clean, cool water
Apply a cool compress
Record what happened and which product
Advise her to see a doctor if it does not settle

blocks.p: Record the client's name and contact details, the date, her skin type, tone and undertone, allergies and patch test results, contraindications checked, the products and shades used, the face chart, any contra-action, and the advice given. She reads and signs it to show she agrees to the service; you sign it too. Keep it private and secure under Jamaica's Data Protection Act.

sections.title: Skin types, skin tones and undertones

head: Skin type
Signs
Products that suit it
rows: Normal
Even, smooth, not shiny or tight; small pores.
Most products; a light moisturiser and primer.
Dry
Tight feeling, fine flakes, dull, small pores; fine lines show more.
Rich moisturiser; hydrating primer; creamy liquid or cream foundation with a dewy or satin finish; little powder; cream blusher.
Oily
Shine, open (enlarged) pores, blackheads, sometimes spots; make-up slides.
Light, oil-free moisturiser; oil-control (mattifying) primer; oil-free matte foundation; powder to set; blotting papers.
Combination
Oily T-zone (forehead, nose and chin); normal or dry cheeks.
Treat each zone: mattifying primer on the T-zone, hydrating on the cheeks; powder mainly on the T-zone.
Sensitive
Reddens, stings or itches easily; may have fine broken veins.
Fragrance-free, gentle products; patch test new products; little rubbing.
Mature
Drier, thinner skin; fine lines and wrinkles; less firm; uneven colour.
Hydrating products in thin layers; cream textures; little powder; matte or satin eyeshadows rather than heavy shimmer.

ul: **Skin tone** is the surface colour, from very fair to very deep. Jamaican clients cover the whole range, so a salon needs foundations, powders and correctors in many shades, including true deep shades.
**Undertone** is the tint beneath the surface: **warm** (golden, yellow, peachy), **cool** (pink, red or bluish), or **neutral** (a mix). Some skins are olive, with a slightly greenish tint.
Rough guides: gold jewellery tends to flatter warm undertones, silver cool ones. Vein colour on the wrist is a poor guide on deeper skin. The jawline test in daylight is the reliable one.

flow: Choose two or three shades that look close
Stripe them on the jawline, running onto the neck
Look in daylight or daylight-balanced light
Wait a few minutes: some foundations darken as they dry
Choose the shade that disappears into the skin of face and neck

ul: Do not test on the back of the hand or the wrist: their colour is often different from the face.

Many deeper skins are not one even colour. They may be darker around the mouth, eyes or forehead and lighter in the centre of the face. Use two shades, or correct the darker areas first and then use the shade that matches most of the face.

Some foundations **oxidise**: oils and pigments react with the air and the skin's oil, and the colour turns darker or more orange after a few minutes. Always check the test stripe again before you choose.

blocks.p: A powder that is too pale, or one made mostly for light skin, can leave a grey, **ashy** look that hides the warmth of brown skin. Use a translucent powder made for deep skin, or a tinted powder that matches or has a warm (golden or 'banana') tone.

head: Term
Meaning
Examples
rows: Primary colours
Colours that cannot be made by mixing others.
Red, yellow and blue.
Secondary colours
Made by mixing two primaries.
Orange (red + yellow), green (yellow + blue), violet (blue + red).
Tertiary colours
Made by mixing a primary with the secondary next to it.
Red-orange, blue-green, yellow-green.
Complementary colours
Opposite each other on the wheel. Mixed, they cancel each other towards brown or grey; side by side, each makes the other look brighter.
Red and green; blue and orange; yellow and violet.
Analogous (harmonious) colours
Next to each other on the wheel; they blend softly.
Orange, red-orange and red.
Warm and cool colours
Warm colours seem to come forward; cool colours seem to move back.
Warm: red, orange, yellow. Cool: blue, green, violet.
Tint, shade and tone
A colour mixed with white (tint), black (shade) or grey (tone).
Pink is a tint of red; maroon is a shade of red.

blocks.p: Correctors use complementary colours to cancel unwanted colour in the skin. Apply them thinly, only where needed, blend the edges, then cover with foundation or concealer.

head: Corrector
Cancels
Use it for
rows: Green
Red
Redness around the nose, spots, flushed patches.
Peach or salmon
Blue and purple
Dark circles on light to medium skin.
Orange or red-orange
Blue, grey and dark brown
Dark circles and dark marks (hyperpigmentation) on deeper skin.
Yellow
Light purple and blue
Mild shadows and small veins on light or medium skin.
Lilac (pale purple)
Yellow
A sallow, yellowish or dull look.

blocks.note: More corrector is not better. A thick patch of green or orange shows through foundation. Use a little, blend it, and check before adding more.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Choose by
Guide
rows: Undertone
Warm undertones often suit golden, bronze, copper, coral and warm red shades. Cool undertones suit pinks, roses, plums, berries and blue-reds. Neutral undertones can wear most colours.
Eye colour

Colours opposite the eye colour on the wheel make it stand out. Brown eyes (a dark orange) are brightened by blue, navy, plum and violet tones, and by bronze and gold; shades that exactly match the eye tend to blend into it.
Outfit
Pick up or complement a colour in the outfit; avoid clashing strong colours.
Occasion and light
Soft, natural colours for day; deeper, stronger or shimmering colours for evening and artificial light.

blocks.p: Corrective make-up uses light and dark to make features look more balanced. The **oval** face is usually taken as the balanced shape: about one and a half times as long as it is wide, with the forehead a little wider than the chin. You correct only what the client wants corrected, and you always blend so that there are no hard lines.

head: Shade
What it does
Use it
rows: Highlight (lighter than the skin)
Brings an area forward and makes it look bigger or wider.
On areas you want to stand out or widen.
Contour or shader (darker than the skin)
Makes an area look smaller, narrower or further back.
On areas you want to slim or set back.

blocks.note: On deeper skin, contour shades should be a little deeper and cooler than the skin, not grey; highlights a little lighter with a golden or warm tone, not chalky white.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Face shape
Looks like
Contour
Highlight and blusher
rows: Oval
Balanced; slightly wider forehead than chin.
Little or none.
Blusher on the cheekbones.
Round
About as wide as it is long; full cheeks; rounded chin.
Under the cheekbones, angled down towards the corners of the mouth, and down the sides of the face at the temples and jaw.
Highlight down the centre: forehead, bridge of the nose, chin. Blusher angled up from the apples towards the temples.
Square
Wide, angular jaw; forehead and jaw about the same width.
The corners of the jaw and the corners of the forehead, to soften the angles.
Highlight the centre of the face. Blusher on the apples, blended up and out in a soft, rounded shape.
Long (oblong)
Much longer than it is wide.
Along the top of the forehead at the hairline, and under the tip of the chin.
Blusher swept across the cheeks, more sideways than up. Highlight the outer cheekbones to add width.
Heart (inverted triangle)
Wide forehead and cheekbones; narrow, pointed chin.
The sides of the forehead at the temples, and lightly on the point of the chin.
Highlight the lower face along the jaw to add width there. Blusher on the apples, blended towards the ears.
Diamond
Narrow forehead and chin; wide cheekbones.
The widest part of the cheekbones.
Highlight the forehead and chin. Blusher on the apples, kept close to the centre.
Pear (triangle)
Narrow forehead; wide jaw.
The sides of the jaw.
Highlight the forehead and temples to widen them. Blusher high on the cheekbones.

head: Eye shape
Aim
Method
rows: Close-set
Make them look further apart.
Keep the inner corners light; add depth at the outer corners and blend outwards; extend liner slightly outwards.
Wide-set
Make them look closer together.
Add depth on the inner part of the lid near the nose; keep the outer corners softer; do not extend liner far outwards; fill the inner ends of the brows.
Hooded
Show more lid.
Place the crease colour slightly above the natural crease, checking with the eyes open; use matte shades; keep liner thin and close to the lashes; curl the lashes.
Deep-set
Bring the eyes forward.
Light or bright colours on the lid; avoid dark colour in the crease; highlight the brow bone lightly.
Prominent (bulging)
Make them look further back.
Matte medium or deep shades over the lid; avoid shimmer on the lid.
Downturned
Lift the outer corner.
Angle shadow and liner upwards at the outer corner; do not drag colour down.

head: Feature
Method
rows: Wide nose
Contour lightly down both sides; a narrow line of highlight down the centre.
Long nose
A little contour under the tip.
Thin lips
Line just on the outer edge of the natural lip line; lighter or brighter colours; a touch of gloss or highlight in the centre.
Full lips
Line exactly on, or just inside, the natural line; matte or deeper shades; avoid heavy gloss.
Uneven lips
Line to balance the two sides, then fill in.
Lips that 'bleed' into fine lines
Line and fill the whole lip with liner as a base; use long-wearing creamy or matte lipstick; avoid gloss at the edges.
Brows

Begin in line with the side of the nostril and the inner corner of the eye; arch above the outer edge of the iris; end on a line from the nostril past the outer corner of the eye. Fill with short, light, hair-like strokes or powder in the direction of growth, then brush through with a spoolie.

head: Product
What it does
Points to know
rows: Primer
Gives a smooth base and helps make-up last.
Hydrating (dry skin), oil-control or mattifying (oily skin), pore-filling, colour-correcting; separate eye and lip primers.
Colour corrector
Cancels unwanted colour.
See the corrector table.
Foundation
Evens the skin tone.
Liquid, cream, stick, powder or tinted moisturiser. Coverage: sheer, medium or full. Finish: matte, satin or dewy. Choose for the skin type and occasion.
Concealer
Covers blemishes, dark marks and dark circles.
Match the skin on blemishes; a shade lighter under the eyes if wanted. Apply thinly and pat in.
Powder
Sets the base and reduces shine.
Loose or pressed; translucent (colourless) or tinted. Press it on lightly with a puff or brush.
Bronzer and contour
Adds warmth (bronzer) or shadow (contour).
Contour is cooler and more matte than bronzer.
Blusher
A natural flush of colour, usually on the apples of the cheeks.
Powder, cream or liquid. Cream suits dry and mature skin.
Highlighter
Brings areas forward and catches light.
Use sparingly for photographs and on textured skin.
Eyeshadow
Colour and shape on the lids.
Finishes: matte, satin, shimmer, metallic, glitter. Use only cosmetic glitter made for the eye area.
Eyeliner
Defines the eye.
Pencil (kohl), gel or liquid.
Mascara
Darkens, thickens and lengthens the lashes.
Waterproof types last through tears and heat but need an oil-based or two-phase remover.
Brow products
Fill and shape the brows.
Pencil, powder, gel or pomade.
Lip liner, lipstick, gloss
Shape, colour and shine.
Liner stops colour bleeding and shapes the lips.
Setting spray
Helps make-up last and look less powdery.
Spray at arm's length, eyes closed, in a ventilated area.

head: Tool
Use
rows: Foundation brush or buffing (kabuki) brush
Applying and blending liquid and cream foundation.
Damp make-up sponge
Pressing in and blending foundation and concealer; single-use in the salon.
Concealer brush
Small, firm brush for precise concealer.
Large soft powder brush
Applying loose powder lightly over the face.
Blusher brush and angled contour brush
Cheek colour; contour under the cheekbones.
Flat eyeshadow brush
Packing colour onto the lid.
Fluffy blending brush and tapered crease brush
Blending edges; placing colour in the crease.
Fine liner brush and angled brush
Gel or liquid liner; brows.
Spoolie
Brushing brows into place; separating lashes.
Lip brush
Applying lipstick evenly.
Lash curler
Curling lashes before mascara; disinfect the pads.
Spatulas, palette, disposable wands, cotton buds
Hygienic product use.

flow: Gown the client and put on a clean headband
Wash your hands
Remove eye and lip make-up with a gentle remover on damp cotton pads
Cleanse with a cleanser for her skin type and remove it fully
Tone to remove the last traces and refresh the skin
Moisturise: richer for dry skin, light and oil-free for oily skin; let it sink in
Apply primer for the skin type; lip balm

blocks.p: Good preparation gives a smooth, clean base, so the make-up goes on evenly and lasts longer, especially in heat and humidity.

flow: Colour corrector
Foundation
Concealer
Cream contour or blusher (if used)
Set with powder
Powder contour, bronzer and blusher
Eye make-up
Brows
Lashes and mascara
Lips
Setting spray

blocks.note: For a heavy or dark smoky eye, many artists do the eyes first, so that fallen powder can be cleaned off before the base goes on. Either order is right if the result is clean and blended.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Apply foundation from the centre of the face outwards, in thin layers, building up only where needed. Blend down past the jawline so there is no line.
Press concealer on with a brush, sponge or ring finger; do not drag it.
Set with a little powder, pressed on lightly. On dry and mature skin use very little, so it does not settle into lines.

flow: Check the eyes are healthy; choose colours
Prime the lids
Sweep a medium shade over the lid
Add a deeper shade in the crease and outer corner; blend up and out with no hard edges
Highlight the brow bone and inner corner
With the client looking down, apply liner close to the upper lashes
Brush away fallen powder from under the eye
Curl the lashes if needed
Apply mascara
Check that both eyes match

head: Eye make-up term
Where it goes
rows: Lid colour
On the moving lid, from the lashes to the crease.
Crease colour
In the fold between the lid and the brow bone, for depth.
Outer corner
A deeper shade, often blended in a sideways 'V'.
Highlight
On the brow bone just under the arch, and sometimes the inner corner.

ul: **Mascara, upper lashes:** the client looks down into a hand mirror held low. Wiggle the wand gently from the roots to the tips. Wipe off excess first, use a new wand for each dip, and comb out clumps.
**Mascara, lower lashes:** the client looks up; use the tip of the wand held upright, lightly.

**Strip lashes:** check the patch test result; measure and trim from the outer end; put a thin line of adhesive on the band, wait until it is tacky, and place it from the centre outwards, close to the lash line.

blocks.note: Never use a pencil, wand or brush near the eye if the client moves suddenly; rest your little finger on her cheek to steady your hand. If any product gets into the eye, rinse with plenty of clean, cool water.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Blusher: ask the client to smile to find the apples of the cheeks; apply lightly and blend towards the hairline, placed to suit the face shape.
Lips: remove the balm; line the lips; fill in with a lip brush; blot with a tissue and apply a second coat for a longer-lasting colour.

blocks.p: Check both sides match in brows, eyes, blusher and lips; that there are no hard lines, tidemarks at the jaw or powder patches; and that the colours look right in daylight. Show the client in a mirror and make any changes she wants.

sections.title: Designing looks for the occasion, aftercare and records

blocks.p: A **face chart** is a printed outline of a face on which you plan and record the look: the products, shades and where each goes, the brushes, and notes. It helps you agree the look with the client, keeps the work on track, and lets you repeat the look exactly, for example on a wedding day after a trial. Keep it with the record card.

head: Look
Seen in
How it is designed
rows: Day
Natural daylight, which shows every detail
Light and natural: a sheer, even base; soft neutral eye colours; a little blusher; natural brows and lips; careful blending.
Evening
Artificial or dim light, which flattens features and dulls colour
Stronger: fuller coverage; contour and highlight; deeper or shimmering eye colours; defined liner; false lashes if wanted; a bolder lip.
Bridal
Daylight, indoor light and photographs, for many hours
Long-wearing and photograph-friendly, usually soft and flattering, designed with the bride for her dress and wishes; waterproof mascara; a well-set base; a trial weeks before.
Photographs and flash
Camera and flash

More definition, as cameras flatten features; matte skin, because heavy shimmer looks like oily shine; avoid large amounts of white-based powders and high-SPF foundations, which can show up white ('flashback'); check a test photo.
Television
Bright studio lights and high-definition cameras
Even, matte, closely matched skin; light layers, because cameras show texture; shine control in the breaks.

head: Client
What to do
rows: Mature skin

Hydrate well; thin layers of light, creamy products; very little powder; matte or satin eyeshadow; crease colour placed above hooded lids; fill sparse brows softly; lip liner to stop bleeding; blusher placed a little higher to lift.
Deeper skin tones
True-shade foundations, often two shades; orange or red-orange correctors for dark marks; powder made for deep skin to avoid an ashy look; rich colours show well.
Men
Usually 'invisible' make-up: a closely matched, sheer, matte base or tinted moisturiser; conceal blemishes; control shine; groom the brows; a clear lip balm. Avoid inflamed razor bumps.
Teenagers
Light, fresh make-up suited to age; oil control where needed; teach good removal habits.

blocks.note: Heat, humidity and sweat break make-up down. For outdoor events use an oil-control primer, long-wearing and waterproof products, light layers set well, and a setting spray, and give the client blotting papers for touch-ups. Weddings, church services, graduations, Carnival and dinners all need different looks: always design for the occasion and the client.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Done some weeks before the wedding, so there is time to change anything and to patch test lash adhesive or new products.
Agree the look, test how it lasts through the day and how it looks in photographs.
Record every product and shade on the face chart, and photograph the result with the bride's agreement.
Plan the timing for the day: how long each person's make-up takes and in what order.
Blot shine with blotting papers instead of piling on powder; avoid touching the face; touch up lips after eating.

Remove all make-up every night: eye make-up first with a gentle remover (an oil-based or two-phase remover for waterproof mascara), then cleanse, tone and moisturise. Sleeping in make-up blocks pores and can cause spots and sore eyes.
Never share mascara, eye pencils or lip products; replace mascara about every three months.
If redness, itching or swelling appears later, remove the make-up and see a doctor or pharmacist if it does not settle.
Wash make-up brushes and sponges at home regularly.

blocks.p: Suggest a product only if it meets the client's needs, such as the primer or lipstick you used today, and explain why it suits her. Tell her the price clearly in J$, never pressure her, and record any advice and sales on her card.

flow: Throw away single-use items in the lined, lidded bin
Sharpener blades and broken blades in the sharps box
Clean brushes, palette and reusable spatulas; disinfect as the makers allow
Disinfect tweezers, lash curler and sharpener
Close and wipe products; store them cool and out of the sun
Wipe the trolley and chair with disinfectant
Gown, towel and headband to the laundry
Complete the record card

ul: I can set up a hygienic workstation with good light and safe equipment.
I can explain cleaning, disinfecting and sterilising and take every product out hygienically, without double-dipping.
I can carry out a consultation and complete and sign a record card.
I can recognise contraindications, refer tactfully and deal with a contra-action.
I can identify skin types, skin tone and undertone, and match foundation on the jawline in daylight.
I can use the colour wheel to choose correctors and colours.
I can identify face shapes and use contour and highlight to balance them.
I can correct close-set, wide-set, hooded and other eye shapes, and thin or full lips.
I can prepare the skin and apply a full make-up in a sensible order, blended and balanced.
I can design day, evening, bridal, photographic and TV looks, and adapt for mature skin, deeper skin and men.
I can plan a look on a face chart.
I can give aftercare and removal advice and recommend products honestly.
I can clean up and store products correctly.

blocks.note: In essays, give the reason with each step: 'I test foundation on the jawline in daylight, because the face and neck must match and artificial light changes colours.'

terms: A private talk before the service to plan the look and check it is safe.
A condition that stops a service or means it must be changed.
An unwanted reaction during or after a service.
A contagious eye infection: red, sore, watery or sticky eye.
A painful, pus-filled lump on the edge of the eyelid.
Blisters near the lips caused by the herpes simplex virus.
Putting a used applicator back into a product.
A small flat tool for taking products out without touching them.
Shows how many months a product can be used after opening.
The surface colour of the skin.
The warm, cool or neutral tint below the surface colour.
Of foundation: to darken or turn orange on the skin after a few minutes.
A grey look on brown skin from a powder or product that is too pale.
Oily in the T-zone, normal or dry on the cheeks.
Colours opposite on the colour wheel, which cancel each other.
A coloured product that cancels unwanted colour in the skin.
A shade lighter than the skin, which brings an area forward.
A shade darker than the skin, which makes an area look smaller or further back.
The balanced face shape, needing little correction.
The fold between the eyelid and the brow bone.
The area just under the arch of the brow.
A brush like a mascara wand, for brows and lashes.
A colourless powder that sets foundation.
A spray that helps make-up last.
White patches in flash photos from some powders and sunscreens.
A face outline on which the look is planned and recorded.
Testing a product on a small area of skin 24 to 48 hours before use.
The inside edge of the eyelid, behind the lashes.

c1.title: A 70th birthday dinner in Black River
c1.text: Mrs. Gloria Henry is celebrating her 70th birthday at a restaurant in Black River at 7 p.m. She has light brown skin with a pinkish, cool undertone, and dry skin with fine lines around her eyes and mouth. Her upper eyelids are hooded and her eyebrows are thin and sparse. Trainee Rushelle is doing her make-up.

c2.title: Three bookings and one brush set in Old Harbour
c2.text: Trainee Kimone has three make-up clients booked one after another at a salon in Old Harbour and only one set of brushes. Her first client, Alicia, tried a new face cream yesterday, and this morning she has a raised, red, itchy rash on both cheeks. Her second client, Tanya, wears contact lenses. Kimone has a pack of make-up sponges and has already used one on a practice model.

c3.title: Morning TV in St Andrew
c3.text: Mr. Andre Lewis, a dark-skinned business presenter, is to appear on a live morning television programme at a studio in St Andrew. His skin is oily and shines under the hot studio lights, and he has razor bumps along his jaw; two are red, with small yellow heads. He asks for make-up 'that nobody can see'. Trainee Marsha-Gaye has 30 minutes and will stay for the programme.

c4.title: Pageant photographs in Falmouth
c4.text: Shantel Gordon, 19, is entering a beauty pageant and needs make-up for her official photographs at a hotel in Falmouth. The photographer will use studio flash. Shantel has medium-brown skin with a warm, golden undertone and dark brown eyes. Her face is heart-shaped: a wide forehead and cheekbones narrowing to a small, pointed chin. Her eyes are set wide apart, and she wants a strong glittery highlight on her cheekbones.

c5.title: A wedding trial in Lucea
c5.text: Natalie Brown is to be married at a beach hotel near Lucea in eight weeks. She comes to the salon with her mother, Mrs. Paulette Brown, for a make-up trial. Natalie has never worn strip false lashes but wants them on the day. Mrs. Brown asks for waterproof mascara because she knows she will cry. Trainee Jodi will record everything on face charts.

questions.q: Which base will suit Mrs. Henry's skin best?
o: A full-coverage matte powder foundation, pressed on thickly
A hydrating liquid foundation in thin layers, little powder
A thick, oil-free foundation set with plenty of loose setting powder
A shimmer foundation all over, to hide the lines with light
questions.why: Dry, mature skin needs moisture and thin layers. Thick matte products and heavy powder sit in fine lines and make them show more; shimmer catches the light on texture rather than hiding it.

questions.q: Where should Rushelle place the crease colour on Mrs. Henry's hooded lids?
o: Exactly in the natural crease, checked with her eyes closed
Over the whole lid right up to the brow, in a frosted shade
A little above the natural crease, checked with eyes open
Only along the lower lash line, so that the hooded lid stays bare
questions.why: On hooded lids the natural crease disappears when the eyes are open, so colour placed in it is hidden. Placing it a little higher, checked with the eyes open, creates visible depth. Matte shades suit mature lids better than frost.

questions.q: Where should Rushelle start each of Mrs. Henry's eyebrows, so they balance her face?
o: Above the centre of each eye, so the eyes look wider apart
In line with the side of the nostril and inner eye corner
Close to the middle of the nose, so the brows nearly meet
Wherever her own hairs start, even if that is far out
questions.why: A balanced brow starts on an upright line from the side of the nostril past the inner corner of the eye, arches above the outer edge of the iris, and ends on a line from the nostril past the outer corner. Fill sparse areas with light, hair-like strokes.

questions.q: Which lip and cheek colours will suit Mrs. Henry's cool undertone best?
o: Warm coral, peach and orange shades
Soft rose, plum and berry shades
Golden bronze and copper shades
Frosted white and pale silver shades
questions.why: Cool undertones have a pink or bluish tint and are flattered by pinks, roses, plums and berries. Corals, bronzes and coppers suit warm undertones, and frosted pale shades look harsh and draw attention to lines on mature skin.

questions.q: What should Kimone do about Alicia's rash?
o: Not make up her face today, and suggest a doctor or pharmacist
Cover the rash with green corrector and a full-coverage foundation
Apply the same new cream again to calm the skin, then carry on
Use only powder products on the cheeks, as powder cannot irritate
questions.why: A new raised, red, itchy rash is probably a reaction to the cream. Putting make-up on it can make it worse, so do not apply products there; explain kindly, suggest she sees a doctor or pharmacist, and record it.

questions.q: How can Kimone use her one set of brushes safely for all three clients?
o: Tap the loose powder out onto a tissue between clients
Rinse them under the tap and use them again while still wet
Clean each with quick-drying brush cleaner between clients
Use them as they are, since each client has fresh products
questions.why: Brushes carry skin oil, make-up and germs from one face to the next. Between clients, clean each brush with a quick-drying brush cleaner as its maker says and let it dry; deep-clean them all at the end of the day. A separate set per client is best.

questions.q: What should Kimone do about Tanya's contact lenses before her eye make-up?
o: Ask her to keep them in, as lenses shield the eyes from powder
Ask if she wants them out, and do not line the inner rim
Refuse all eye make-up, as lenses always stop the service
Wet the lenses with saline so the powder slides off them
questions.why: Lenses are not a contraindication, but particles caught behind a lens irritate the eye. Let the client choose whether to remove them, avoid the waterline, tap off loose powder and avoid loose glitter or fibre mascara.

questions.q: What should Kimone do with the make-up sponge she has already used on the practice model?
o: Rinse it in water and use it damp for Alicia
Throw it away; use a new one for each client
Let it dry in the hot sun so that the germs on it die
Spray it with setting spray and use it again
questions.why: Sponges are porous and soak up product, oil and germs, and they cannot be disinfected reliably in a busy salon. Treat them as single-use and throw them away after each client.

questions.q: What look suits Mr. Lewis best?
o: A sheer, matte, matched base that evens tone and stops shine
A full contour and highlight, so his face shows up on camera
A pale powder all over, so the lights do not make him look dark
A dewy, shimmering base to give his skin a healthy TV glow
questions.why: He wants make-up nobody can see. A thin, closely matched, matte base evens the tone and controls shine under hot lights. Heavy contour shows on a high-definition camera, pale powder looks ashy on dark skin, and shimmer reads as oily shine.

questions.q: What should Marsha-Gaye do about the two red razor bumps with yellow heads?
o: Squeeze them gently with clean tissues, then conceal them
Cover them thickly with concealer so they do not show
Avoid them: no product or brushes over the bumps
Press setting powder into them to dry them out
questions.why: Bumps with yellow heads are infected. Squeezing or covering them can spread infection and make them worse, and a brush that touches them carries germs to the rest of the face. Work around them and suggest he sees a doctor if they keep coming.

questions.q: Halfway through the programme, Mr. Lewis's forehead is shining again. What is the best quick fix in the break?
o: Add another layer of foundation over the shiny area
Wipe it with a damp sponge and leave it to air-dry
Spray moisturiser over it to even out the shine
Press on a blotting paper, then a little powder
questions.why: Blotting lifts the oil first; a light press of powder then sets the area again. Adding powder or foundation over oil builds a cakey layer that shows on camera.

questions.q: Where should the contour shade go to balance Shantel's heart-shaped face?
o: Along both corners of the jaw, to make the lower face narrower
At the sides of the forehead and lightly on the chin
Down the centre of the forehead, the nose and the chin
In a round circle on the apples of the cheeks, blended upward
questions.why: A heart-shaped face is widest at the forehead and cheekbones and narrow at the chin. Contour at the temples narrows the top; a little on the point of the chin softens it; highlight along the jaw adds width below.

questions.q: Which eye make-up method helps Shantel's wide-set eyes look a little closer together?
o: Keep the inner corners bright and darken the outer corners
Extend the eyeliner well past the outer corners in a long wing
Add depth on the inner part of the lid, near the nose
Use one pale shade only, with no liner and no mascara
questions.why: Darker colour seems to move back and draw the eye. Depth near the nose pulls the eyes visually inwards. Brightening the inner corners and extending liner outwards does the opposite, which is the method for close-set eyes.

questions.q: Which eyeshadow colours would make Shantel's dark brown eyes stand out most?
o: Navy, plum and violet tones, which contrast with brown
Brown shades that exactly match the colour of her eyes
Black only, all over the lid and up to the brow bone
Pale grey and white, to lighten the whole eye area
questions.why: Brown is a dark orange. Colours on the opposite side of the wheel, blues and violets, make it look richer. Matching browns blend in, black all over closes the eye, and grey and white look ashy on warm brown skin.

questions.q: Why should the artist take care with Shantel's strong glittery highlight for the flash photographs?
o: Heavy shimmer can look like oily shine in flash photos
Glitter makes the flash too weak to light her whole face
Flash melts shimmer products and makes them slide off
Shimmer turns green under flash and looks like a bruise
questions.why: Flash bounces off shimmer and glitter, and in photos large areas of it look like sweat or grease. Keep highlight to a small area, check a test shot, and keep the rest of the skin matte.

questions.q: Natalie has never worn strip lashes. What should Jodi do about the lash adhesive?
o: Put the lashes on at the trial with extra glue to test it
Skip any test, as lash glue never touches the skin
Patch test the adhesive 24 to 48 hours before it is used
Test the glue on Jodi's own arm instead of Natalie's
questions.why: Lash adhesive can cause allergic reactions, and some contain latex. A patch test on the client's own skin 24 to 48 hours before first use, as the Centre's policy says, shows whether she reacts, well before the wedding.

questions.q: Why is the make-up trial done weeks before the wedding?
o: So the bride can buy every product the artist used on her
To agree the look, and see how it lasts and photographs
So the price can be raised if the full look takes longer
To use up old stock before the busy wedding season starts
questions.why: The trial lets the bride and artist agree the look, test how it wears in the heat and in photos, patch test new products and change anything in good time. The face chart records it so it can be repeated on the day.

questions.q: What should Jodi tell Mrs. Brown about removing waterproof mascara?
o: Scrub the lashes with soap and hot water until it comes off
Leave it on for a few days until it flakes off by itself
Use an oil-based or two-phase eye remover, gently
Pull it off the lashes with a cotton pad soaked in toner
questions.why: Waterproof mascara resists water, so soap and toner will not shift it; scrubbing and pulling damage the lashes and irritate the eyes. An oil-based or two-phase remover dissolves it; hold the pad on the lashes for a few seconds, then wipe gently.

questions.q: A client's foundation matched her jaw perfectly, but 15 minutes later it looks darker and slightly orange. What has most likely happened?
o: The powder has reacted with the primer
The foundation has oxidised on her skin
Her undertone has changed in the warm room
The shade was tested in too much daylight
questions.why: Some foundations oxidise: their oils and pigments react with air and skin oil and darken after application. Wait a few minutes after a test stripe before choosing, and pick a shade that allows for it.

questions.q: Which corrector colour is usually used to cancel a sallow, yellowish look on the skin?
o: Mint green
Orange or peach
Pale yellow
Lilac (pale purple)
questions.why: Yellow and violet are opposite each other on the colour wheel, so a thin layer of lilac cancels a yellowish tone. Green cancels redness, and orange or peach cancels blue and dark tones.
